title: Jeremiah Pharoah, Montaukett Whaler
summary: Jeremiah Pharoah was a Montaukett deep-sea whaler whose life connected Indian Fields, Nantucket, Sag Harbor, Samson Occom's book history, and archaeological evidence from his household. McGovern's research connects him with whaling out of Nantucket, his 1794 marriage to Aloosa / Lois Tallman, his 1798 return to Montauk, and household material culture at Indian Fields.
content:
Jeremiah Pharoah was a Montaukett deep-sea whaler whose life connected Indian Fields, Nantucket, Sag Harbor, Samson Occom's book history, and the material record of his household. Sources document his return to Montauk in 1798, but they do not establish exact birth or death dates.

Historical context

Jeremiah Pharoah recorded family and life events inside a book formerly associated with Samson Occom. A later newspaper transcription preserves a first-person statement in which he described sailing the world for nine years and returning home to find his relations struggling. Archaeological research also connects his household with a scrimshaw knife handle bearing his name.

"I Jeremiah Pharaoh the Bold mariner I sailed the world all over nine long years. When I Returned home I found my relations stranded which grieved my heart ful so."

Indian Fields carries sensitive archaeological and community history, so household and archaeological locations are not identified.

References

  • Allison Manfra McGovern, Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montaukett, 2015.
  • Allison Manfra McGovern, "The Materiality of a Bold Mariner," source context for Jeremiah Pharoah's book inscription and household material culture.
  • Sag Harbor Express, July 31, 1924, transcription of Jeremiah Pharoah material cited by McGovern.
  • Gaynell Stone, The History and Archaeology of the Montauk.
why_this_matters: Jeremiah Pharoah's life shows Montaukett maritime labor as global, literate, and deeply tied to family and homeland. His own recorded words, whaling history, and household material culture challenge any idea that Native Long Island history ended with colonial land loss.
